title: Of presumption
paragraphs: There is another kind of glory — having too good an opinion of our own worth. It is a thoughtless self-love that flatters us, and represents us to ourselves as other than we truly are; like the passion of love, which lends beauties and graces to its object, and makes those caught up in it, with corrupted judgment, consider the thing they love other than it is and more perfect than it is.

I would not, however, for fear of erring on this side, that a man should fail to know himself properly, or think himself less than he is. The judgment ought in all things to keep its rights; it is only reasonable that he should discern in himself, as in others, what truth places before him. If he is Caesar, let him boldly think himself the greatest captain in the world. We are nothing but ceremony: ceremony carries us along and we leave behind the substance of things; we hold onto the branches and let go the trunk and the body. We have taught the ladies to blush when they hear that named which they are not at all afraid to do; we dare not call our members by their right names, yet are not afraid to put them to every kind of debauchery. Ceremony forbids us to express in words what is lawful and natural, and we obey it; reason forbids us to do what is unlawful and wrong, and nobody obeys it. I find myself here hampered by the laws of ceremony, for it permits a man neither to speak well of himself nor ill; we will leave it there for now.

Those whom fortune (call it good or ill) has set in some prominent station can show by their public actions what they are; but those she has only employed in the crowd, of whom no one will say a word unless they speak for themselves, are to be excused if they take the liberty of speaking about themselves to people who have an interest in knowing them — on the precedent of Lucilius:
"Ille velut fidis arcana sodalibus olim Credebat libris, neque si male cesserat, usquam Decurrens alio, neque si bene: quo fit, ut omnis, Votiva pateat veluri descripta tabella Vita senis;"

["He used formerly to confide his secret thoughts to his books, as to tried friends, and resorted to no other refuge, in good times or ill: so it comes about that the old man's whole life is laid out there as on a votive tablet." — Horace, Sat., ii. 1, 30.]
He always committed his actions and his thoughts to paper, and portrayed himself there exactly as he found himself to be:
"Nec id Rutilio et Scauro citra fidem; aut obtrectationi fuit."
["Nor was this thought a breach of good faith or a thing damaging to Rutilius or Scaurus." — Tacitus, Agricola, c. 1.]

I remember, then, that from my infancy I was observed to carry myself in a way, I don't know quite how, that smacked of pride and arrogance. Let me say by the way that it is not unreasonable to suppose we have qualities and inclinations so much our own, so deeply rooted in us, that we have no way of feeling and recognising them; and that the body keeps a certain bent from such natural inclinations without our knowledge or consent. It was an affectation of a piece with his beauty that made Alexander carry his head on one side, and made Alcibiades lisp; Julius Caesar scratched his head with one finger, which is the trick of a man full of worrying thoughts; and Cicero, as I recall, used to wrinkle his nose, the sign of a man given to mocking. Such tics may take hold in us without our noticing. There are other, artificial ones I won't get into — bows and salutations, by which men acquire (often undeservedly) the reputation of being humble and courteous; one can be humble out of pride. I am prodigal enough with my hat, especially in summer, and never receive a salute without returning it, from people of any rank, unless they are in my own service. I should make it a request to some princes I know that they be more sparing of that ceremony, and bestow it where it is more due, for being so indiscriminately conferred on everyone, it is thrown away to no purpose; if it is given without respect of persons, it loses its effect. Among irregular forms of bearing, let us not forget that haughty one of the Emperor Constantius, who always in public held his head upright and stiff, without bending or turning to either side, not even to look at those who saluted him from one side; planting his body in a rigid, motionless posture, not letting it yield to the motion of his coach, not daring even to spit, blow his nose, or wipe his face in front of others. I don't know whether the gestures observed in me belonged to this first category, or whether I really had some hidden tendency to this vice, as may well have been the case; I cannot be held accountable for the motions of the body. But as to the motions of the soul, I must confess here what I think of the matter.

This glory consists of two parts: one in setting too high a value on ourselves, the other in setting too low a value on others. As to the first, these considerations should, it seems to me, carry some weight. I find myself plagued by an error of the soul that displeases me, both as unjust and, still more, as a nuisance: I try to correct it but cannot root it out. It is this — I undervalue the just worth of things I possess and overvalue things because they are foreign, absent, and not mine. This trait spreads widely. Just as the prerogative of authority makes husbands look on their own wives with a culpable disdain, and many fathers look on their children that way, so I, between two equal merits, would always tilt against my own — not so much that the jealousy of my own advancement clouds my judgment and stops me from satisfying myself, as that possession in itself breeds contempt for what it holds and governs. Foreign governments, manners, and languages insinuate themselves into my esteem; I can feel that Latin entices me, by the favour of its dignity, to value it above its due, as it does with children and ordinary people. My neighbour's household management, house, and horse, though no better than my own, I prize above my own because they are not mine. Besides being very ignorant in my own affairs, I am struck by the confidence everyone else has in himself: whereas there is scarcely anything I am sure I know, or that I can guarantee myself I can do. I do not have my means of doing things ready and on tap, and only know what they are after the fact; I am as doubtful of my own strength as of another's. So it happens that if I do something commendable, I attribute it more to my fortune than to my industry, since I plan everything by chance and with hesitation. I have this, too, in general: of all the opinions antiquity has held of men en masse, I most willingly embrace those that most despise and undervalue us, and most push us towards nothing. Philosophy has never, it seems to me, so fair a field to play on as when it falls on our vanity and presumption, when it most exposes our irresolution, weakness, and ignorance. I take the too-good opinion that man has of himself to be the nursing mother of all the most false opinions, both public and private. Those people who ride astride upon the epicycle of Mercury, who see so far into the heavens, are worse to me than a tooth-drawer come to draw my teeth; for in my own study, the subject of which is man, finding such variety of judgments, so profound a labyrinth of difficulties piled on each other, so much diversity and uncertainty even in the very school of wisdom itself — you may judge, since these people could not settle on the knowledge of themselves and their own condition, which is continually before their eyes and within them, since they do not know what moves what they themselves move, nor how to describe to us the springs they themselves work and use — how can I trust them about the ebbing and flowing of the Nile? The curiosity to know things was given to man as a scourge, says Holy Scripture.

But to come back to what concerns me. I think it would be very difficult for any other man to have a meaner opinion of himself — and just as difficult for another to have a meaner opinion of me than I do. I take myself for one of the common run, except in this: that I have no better an opinion of myself; guilty of the meanest, most ordinary defects, but neither denying them nor making excuses; and I value myself on no other account than that I know my own value. If there is any vanity in me, it is superficially infused by the treachery of my temperament, with no body to it that my judgment can discern. I am sprinkled, but not dyed. As for the productions of the mind, there is no part of me, whatever it is, that I am content with; and others' approval does not raise my opinion of myself. My judgment is tender and exacting, especially in things that concern me.

I am always disowning myself, feeling myself float and waver because of my weakness. I have nothing of my own that satisfies my judgment. My eyesight is clear and steady enough, but when it gets to work, it is apt to be dazzled — as I find most plainly in poetry. I love poetry to distraction, and can pass a tolerable judgment on others' work; but in good earnest, when I apply myself to it, I play the child and cannot bear myself. A man may play the fool in anything else, but not in poetry:
"Mediocribus esse poetis Non dii, non homines, non concessere columnae."
["Neither gods, nor men, nor booksellers' pillars (on which poets posted their works) tolerate mediocrity in poets." — Horace, De Arte Poet., 372.]
I wish to God this line were written over the doors of all our printers, to forbid entry to so many rhymesters!
"Verum Nihil securius est malo poetae."
["The truth is, nothing is more self-assured than a bad poet." — Martial, xii. 63, 13.]

Why do we not have such people? Dionysius the elder prided himself on nothing so much as his poetry. At the Olympic games, with chariots surpassing all the rest in magnificence, he also sent poets and musicians to present his verses, with tents and pavilions royally gilt and hung with tapestry. When his verses came to be recited, the excellence of the delivery at first held the people's attention; but when they came afterwards to weigh the cheapness of the composition, they first slid into disdain, and as their judgments were stung further, they passed into fury, and ran to pull down and tear to pieces all his pavilions. And when his chariots failed in the race, and the ship that was to bring his people home missed Sicily and was driven by the storm onto the coast of Tarentum, they were certain it was through the anger of the gods, incensed (as they themselves were) at the paltry poem. Even the sailors who escaped the wreck backed this opinion of the people, and the oracle that foretold his death seemed to agree: "Dionysius will be near his end when he has overcome those who are better than himself." He interpreted this of the Carthaginians, who surpassed him in power, and being at war with them, often turned aside from victory to avoid running into the prophecy. But he misunderstood it: the god was indicating the time of the advantage he obtained at Athens, by favour and injustice, over the tragic poets — better than he — by having his own play, called the Leneians, performed in competition. Right after that victory he died, partly from the excessive joy he felt at the success.
[Diodorus Siculus, xv. 7. The play, however, was called the "Ransom of Hector." It was the games at which it was performed that were called Lenaean; they were one of the four Dionysiac festivals.]

What I find tolerable in my own work is not really so in itself, but only by comparison with worse things that I see receive a perfectly good reception. I envy the happiness of those who can please and hug themselves over what they do; for it is an easy pleasure, since a man draws it from himself, especially if he is steady in his self-conceit. I know a poet against whom the intelligent and the ignorant, abroad and at home, both heaven and earth cry out that he has very little notion of the thing — and yet for all that he has not the slightest worse opinion of himself; he is always launching some new piece, contriving some new invention, and persists in his opinion all the more obstinately, since it is only he who has to maintain it.
My works please me so little that whenever I look them over again, they disgust me:
"Cum relego, scripsisse pudet; quia plurima cerno, Me quoque, qui feci, judice, digna lini."
["When I re-read what I have written, I am ashamed, for I see many passages that I, the author, being the judge, think should be erased." — Ovid, De Ponto, i. 5, 15.]

I always have an idea in my soul, a sort of confused image that presents itself to me as in a dream, in a better form than the one I have used; but I cannot catch it or fit it to my purpose. And even that idea is only a middling one. From this I conclude that the productions of those great rich souls of former times are far beyond the utmost stretch of my imagination or my wish; their writings not only satisfy and fill me, they astound me and ravish me with admiration. I judge their beauty; I see it, if not to the utmost, then so far at least as it is possible for me to aim. Whatever I undertake, I owe a sacrifice to the Graces — as Plutarch says of someone else — to win their favour:
"Si quid enim placet, Si quid dulce horninum sensibus influit, Debentur lepidis omnia Gratiis."
["If anything pleases that I write, if anything sweet flows into men's minds, all is due to the charming Graces." The verses are probably by some modern poet.]

They abandon me throughout; all I write is rough, polish and beauty are lacking; I cannot set things off to advantage; my handling adds nothing to the material — so my material had better be forceful, very full, and have a lustre of its own. If I pick subjects that are popular and lively, it is to follow my own bent, since I do not affect a solemn, ceremonious wisdom as the world does, and to keep myself more sprightly — not my style more loose, which would rather have things grave and severe (at least if I may call "style" what is in fact an unformed and irregular way of speaking, a popular jargon, a procedure without definition, division, or conclusion, perplexed like that of Amafanius and Rabirius). I can neither please, nor delight, nor even tickle my readers; the best story in the world is spoiled by my handling and goes flat. I can only speak in rough earnest, and am entirely lacking that easy facility I observe in many of my acquaintances, of entertaining the first comer and keeping a whole company going, or holding a prince's ear with all kinds of talk without tiring themselves out. They never lack matter, thanks to the gift and grace they have of seizing on the first thing that comes up and adjusting it to the humour and capacity of the people they are with. Princes are not much fond of solid discourse, and I am not fond of telling stories. The first and easiest reasons, which are usually those best received, I do not know how to deploy: I am a bad orator for the common sort. I tend to say on every topic the extremest thing I know. Cicero thinks that in treatises of philosophy the opening is the hardest part; if that is true, I am wise to stick to the conclusion. And yet one ought to know how to tune the string to every note, and the highest is the one least often touched. There is at least as much skill in raising up an empty subject as in carrying a weighty one. A man must sometimes handle things superficially, sometimes push them home. I know perfectly well that most people stay at this lower level because they cannot conceive of things otherwise than through this outer bark; but I also know that the greatest masters — Xenophon and Plato — are often seen stooping to this low and popular manner of speaking and treating of things, but holding it up with graces that never fail them.

Further, my language has nothing facile or polished in it; it is rough, free, irregular, and as such pleases — if not my judgment, at least my inclination. But I see clearly that I sometimes give myself too much rein, and that in trying to avoid art and affectation I fall into the opposite trouble:
"Brevis esse laboro, Obscurus fio."
["Trying to be brief, I become obscure." — Horace, Art. Poet., 25.]

Plato says that length or brevity are not the properties that take value from language or give it. Even if I tried to follow the other, more moderate, even, regular style, I should never get there; and although the short, rounded periods of Sallust best suit my temperament, I find Caesar much grander and harder to imitate. And though my inclination would rather prompt me to imitate Seneca's manner of writing, I nevertheless esteem Plutarch's more. In both doing and speaking, I simply follow my own natural way, which is perhaps why I am better at speaking than writing. Motion and action animate words, especially in those who lay about them briskly, as I do, and grow hot. Bearing, expression, voice, robe, place — all these will set off some things that on their own would seem little more than chatter. Messalla complains in Tacitus about the tightness of certain garments in his time, and about the design of the benches where the orators had to declaim, which were a disadvantage to their eloquence.

My French is corrupted, both in pronunciation and otherwise, by the barbarism of my country. I have never seen a man from any of the provinces on this side of the kingdom whose speech did not betray his birthplace, and was not offensive to ears that were purely French. Yet it is not that I am perfect in my own Périgord dialect either: I can no more speak it than High Dutch, nor do I much care. It is a language (like the others around me on every side — Poitou, Xaintonge, Angoumois, Limousin, Auvergne) — a poor, drawling, scurvy tongue. Above us towards the mountains there is, however, a sort of Gascon spoken that I am much taken with: blunt, brief, telling, and in truth a more manly and military language than any other I know, as sinewy, powerful, and pertinent as French is graceful, neat, and luxuriant.

As for Latin, which was given me as my mother tongue, I have through disuse lost the practice of speaking it, and indeed of writing it too — though I once had a particular reputation in it; by which you may see how unremarkable I am on that side.

Beauty counts for a great deal in our dealings with each other; it is the first means of winning others' favour and goodwill, and no man is so barbarous and morose as not to feel himself in some sort touched by its appeal. The body has a great share in our being, has a prominent place in it, and so its structure and composition are well worth considering. Those who try to disjoin and separate our two principal parts from one another are mistaken; on the contrary, we ought to reunite and join them. We must order the soul not to withdraw and entertain itself apart, not to despise and abandon the body (which she cannot really do anyway, but only by some apish counterfeit), but to bind herself close to it, to embrace, cherish, assist, govern, and advise it, and to bring it back into the right way when it strays — in short, to marry it and be its husband, so that their effects appear not divergent and contrary but uniform and concurrent. Christians have a particular instruction on this connection, for they know that the divine justice embraces this fellowship and joining of body and soul, even to the point of making the body capable of eternal rewards; and that God has an eye on the whole man's ways, and wills that he receive entire chastisement or reward, according to his merits or demerits. The school of the Peripatetics, of all schools the most sociable, attributes to wisdom this single care: to provide equally for the good of these two associated parts. The other schools, in not sufficiently applying themselves to this mixture, show themselves to be divided — one for the body and the other for the soul, with equal error — and to have lost sight of their subject, which is Man, and of their guide, which they generally confess to be Nature. The first distinction ever drawn among men, and the first consideration that gave some pre-eminence over others, was likely the advantage of beauty:
"Agros divisere atque dedere Pro facie cujusque, et viribus ingenioque; Nam facies multum valuit, viresque vigebant."
["They distributed and assigned the lands according to each man's beauty, strength, and understanding; for beauty counted for much, and strength was in favour." — Lucretius, V. 1109.]

Now, I am of slightly less than middling stature — a defect that not only borders on deformity but carries with it a real inconvenience, especially for those in office and in command, for the authority that a graceful presence and a majestic bearing inspire is lacking. C. Marius would not willingly enlist soldiers who were not six feet tall. The Courtier has reason to prefer a moderate stature in the gentlemen he is presenting, and to reject any oddity that would make him be pointed at. But if I had to choose whether the middle should lean below or above the common standard, I would not have it lean below in a soldier. Small men, says Aristotle, are pretty, but not handsome; and greatness of soul is shown in a great body, as beauty is in a tall stature. The Ethiopians and Indians, he says, considered the beauty and stature of their persons when they chose their kings and magistrates. They had good reason for it: it inspires respect in those who follow him, and is a terror to the enemy, to see a leader of brave and goodly stature marching at the head of a battalion:
"Ipse inter primos praestanti corpore Turnus Vertitur arma, tenens, et toto vertice supra est."
["In the front rank marches Turnus, brandishing his weapon, taller by a head than all the rest." — Virgil, Aeneid, vii. 783.]
Our holy and heavenly king, every circumstance of whom is to be observed with the greatest care, religion, and reverence, has not himself rejected this bodily recommendation:
"Speciosus forma prae filiis hominum."
["He is fairer than the children of men." — Psalm xliv. 3.]

And Plato, along with temperance and fortitude, requires beauty in the guardians of his republic. It would vex you if someone came to you among your servants asking where Monsieur is, and the only thing you got out of the salutation was the remnant that was paid to your barber or your secretary — as happened to poor Philopoemen, who, having arrived first of his party at an inn where he was expected, was set by the hostess, who didn't know him and saw him an unsightly fellow, to help her maids draw water and make a fire against Philopoemen's coming. The gentlemen of his suite arrived soon after, and surprised to see him at this fine work — for he had not failed to obey his landlady's command — asked him what he was doing. "I am," he said, "paying the penalty of my ugliness." The other beauties belong to women; stature is the only beauty proper to men. Where the stature is contemptible, no width or roundness of forehead, no whiteness and sweetness of eyes, no moderate proportion of nose, no smallness of ears or mouth, no evenness and whiteness of teeth, no thickness of well-set brown beard shining like a chestnut husk, no curled hair, no exact proportion of head, no fresh complexion, no pleasing air of face, no body free of offensive scent, no perfect proportion of limbs, can make a handsome man. As for the rest, I am strongly and tightly built; my face is not puffy but full, and my complexion is between jovial and melancholic, moderately sanguine and hot —
"Unde rigent setis mihi crura, et pectora villis;"
["From which my legs and breast bristle with hair." — Martial, ii. 36, 5.]

my health robust and sprightly even to a well-advanced age, rarely troubled by illness. So I was, for I do not now make any account of myself, being engaged in the avenues of old age, already past forty:
"Minutatim vires et robur adultum Frangit, et in partem pejorem liquitur aetas:"
["By degrees, age breaks our strength and full-grown vigour, and melts us into the worse part." — Lucretius, ii. 1131.]
What I shall be from now on will only be half a being, and no more me; every day I slip away and steal from myself:
"Singula de nobis anni praedantur euntes."
["The passing years each steal something from us." — Horace, Ep., ii. 2.]

Agility and skill I never had — and yet I am the son of a very active, sprightly father, who continued so to an extreme old age. I have scarcely known anyone of his condition who was his equal in all bodily exercises, just as I have seldom met anyone who did not surpass me, except in running, at which I was pretty good. In music and singing — for which I have a very unfit voice — and in playing any kind of instrument, they could never teach me anything. In dancing, tennis, and wrestling, I could never get beyond an ordinary level; in swimming, fencing, vaulting, and leaping, to no level at all. My hands are so clumsy I can hardly write so as to read it myself, so that I would rather do over again what I have scribbled than take the trouble to make it out. I read scarcely better than I write, and feel that I weary my hearers in the bargain. Otherwise I am not a bad clerk. I cannot fold a letter neatly, nor could I ever make a pen, nor carve at table worth a pin, nor saddle a horse, nor carry a hawk and fly her, nor work the dogs, nor lure a hawk, nor speak to a horse. In short, my bodily qualities suit those of my soul: there is nothing sprightly, only a steady, firm vigour. I am patient enough of labour and pains, but only when I go to it voluntarily, and only as long as my own desire urges me to:
"Molliter austerum studio fallente laborem."
["Studious application softly beguiling severe labour." — Horace, Sat., ii. 2, 12.]

Otherwise, if I am not enticed by some pleasure, or led by some guide other than my own pure and free inclination, I am good for nothing. For I am of a humour where, life and health excepted, there is nothing for which I will bite my nails, or buy at the price of mental torment and constraint:
"Tanti mihi non sit opaci Omnis arena Tagi, quodque in mare volvitur aurum."
["I would not buy at that price the sands of dark Tagus, or all the gold that rolls down to the sea." — Juvenal, Sat., iii. 54.]

Extremely idle, extremely given up to my own inclination, both by nature and by art, I would as willingly lend a man my blood as my labour. I have a soul that is free, and entirely its own, and accustomed to guide itself in its own fashion; never having had master or governor imposed on me, I have walked as far as I would, at the pace that best pleased me. This is what has made me unfit for the service of others, and useful to no one but myself.

Nor was there any need to force my heavy, lazy disposition; for being born to a fortune I had reason to be content with (a reason, nevertheless, that a thousand others of my acquaintance would have used as a plank to step across in search of a higher fortune, into tumult and disquiet), and with as much intelligence as I needed, I sought no more, and got no more:
"Non agimur tumidis velis Aquilone secundo, Non tamen adversis aetatem ducimus Austris Viribus, ingenio, specie, virtute, loco, re, Extremi primorum, extremis usque priores."

["The north wind does not swell our sails, nor does Auster trouble our course with storms. In strength, talent, looks, virtue, rank, and wealth, we fall short of the foremost, but stand ahead of the last." — Horace, Ep., ii. 2, 201.]

All I needed was enough to keep me content; which, rightly considered, is a discipline of soul equally difficult in every kind of condition, and one we are apt to see more readily in want than in abundance — perhaps because, on the analogy of our other passions, the desire for riches is sharpened more by their use than by the need of them; and the virtue of moderation is rarer than that of patience. I never had anything to desire but to enjoy happily the estate that God in His bounty had put into my hands. I have never known what trouble is, and have had little to do with anything but the management of my own affairs; or, if I have had other business, it was on condition of doing it at my own leisure, in my own way, entrusted to me by people who had confidence in me, who did not press me, and who knew my temperament; for good horsemen can get service out of a broken-winded jade.

Even my infancy was brought up in a gentle and free way, exempt from any rigorous subjection. All this has helped me to a delicate temperament, incapable of worry, to the point that I love to have my losses and the troubles I am caught up in concealed from me. In the account of my expenses, I put down what my negligence costs me to feed and maintain it:
"Haec nempe supersunt, Quae dominum fallunt, quae prosunt furibus."
["That surplus which the owner does not know of, but which benefits the thieves." — Horace, Ep., i. 645.]

I prefer not to know what I have, so that I am less sensitive to its loss. I ask those who serve me, when affection and integrity are lacking, to deceive me with a decent appearance at least. Lacking the steadiness to bear the shock of adverse accidents to which we are exposed, and the patience to apply myself seriously to the management of my affairs, I nourish in myself as much as I can this rule — leaving everything to fortune, "to take things at the worst, and resolve to bear that worst with calm and patience"; that is all I aim at, and to that I direct all my meditation. In a danger, I do not so much consider how I shall escape it as how little it matters whether I escape it or not — should I be left dead on the spot, what of it? Not being able to govern events, I govern myself, and apply myself to them, if they will not apply themselves to me. I have no great art for evading or escaping or forcing fortune, and steering things to my own bias by foresight. I have even less patience for the troublesome, painful care that requires. The most uneasy condition for me is to be suspended on urgent occasions, and to be agitated between hope and fear.

Deliberation, even in matters of the slightest moment, is very troublesome to me; and my mind finds it harder to undergo the various tumblings and tossings of doubt and consultation than to settle down and acquiesce in whatever happens once the die is cast. Few passions break my sleep; deliberations the least of all do it. On the road I prefer to avoid the sloping and slippery paths, and put myself onto the well-trodden track, however muddy and deep, where I can fall no lower, and there look for my safety. So I love misfortunes that are purely so — that do not torment and tease me with the uncertainty of their growing better, but that at the first push plunge me directly into the worst that can be expected.
"Dubia plus torquent mala."
["Doubtful ills are the worst torture." — Seneca, Agamemnon, iii. 1, 29.]

In events I bear myself like a man; in conduct, like a child. The fear of the fall gives me more fever than the fall itself. The game is not worth the candle. The miser fares worse with his passion than the poor man, and the jealous man worse than the cuckold; a man often loses more by defending his vineyard than by giving it up. The lowest walk is the safest; it is the seat of constancy. There you need no one but yourself; there you are founded and standing entirely on your own base. Has not this example, of a gentleman well known, some hint of philosophy in it? He married, well advanced in years, having spent his youth in good fellowship, a great talker and a great mocker, recalling how much the subject of cuckoldry had given him occasion to talk and scoff at others. To stop them paying him back in his own coin, he married a wife from a place where any man finds what he wants for his money: "Good morning, strumpet"; "Good morning, cuckold" — and there was nothing he more commonly and openly entertained his visitors with than this design of his, by which he stopped the private muttering of mockers and blunted the point of the reproach.

As for ambition — which is neighbour, or rather daughter, to presumption — for it to advance me, fortune would have had to come and take me by the hand. To bestir myself for an uncertain hope, and submit myself to all the difficulties that come with those who are trying to push themselves into credit at the beginning of their career, I could never have done it:
"Spem pretio non emo."
["I will not buy hope at any price" (or, "I do not purchase hope at a price"). — Terence, Adelphi, ii. 3, 11.]
I apply myself to what I see and to what I have in hand, and do not go very far from the shore,
"Alter remus aquas, alter tibi radat arenas:"
["One oar plunging into the sea, the other raking the sands." — Propertius, iii. 3, 23.]

and besides, a man rarely comes by such promotions without first hazarding what he has of his own; and I am of the opinion that if a man has enough to keep him in the station he was born and brought up in, it is great folly to risk that on the chance of increasing it. The man to whom fortune has denied the means to set his foot on a quiet, settled way of life is to be excused if he stakes what he has, since whatever happens, necessity drives him to shift for himself:
"Capienda rebus in malis praeceps via est:"
["In bad cases a course must be taken" (or, "A desperate case requires a desperate course"). — Seneca, Agamemnon, ii. 1, 47.]

and I am readier to excuse a younger brother for exposing what his friends have left him to the mercy of fortune than the heir on whose shoulders the honour of his family rests, who cannot be needy except by his own fault. I have found a much shorter and easier way, by the advice of the good friends I had in my younger days, to free myself from any such ambition, and to sit still:
"Cui sit conditio dulcis sine pulvere palmae:"
["What condition can compare with that of one who has won the palm without the dust of the race?" — Horace, Ep., i. 1, 51.]

judging soundly enough of my own strength that it was not equal to any great matters, and remembering the saying of the late Chancellor Olivier, that the French were like monkeys swarming up a tree from branch to branch, and never stopping until they reach the very top, where they show their behinds.
"Turpe est, quod nequeas, capiti committere pondus, Et pressum inflexo mox dare terga genu."
["It is shameful to load the head with what it cannot bear, the knees soon giving way under the weight." — Propertius, iii. 9, 5.]

Even the best qualities I have would, I find, be useless in this age. The easiness of my manners would have been called weakness and negligence; my faith and conscience, scrupulousness and superstition; my liberty and freedom, troublesome, thoughtless, and rash. Bad luck is good for something. It is a good thing to be born into a very depraved age, for, by comparison with others, you will be reckoned virtuous cheaply: in our day, a man who is only a parricide and a sacrilegious person is an honest man and a man of honour:
"Nunc, si depositum non inficiatur amicus, Si reddat veterem cum tota aerugine follem, Prodigiosa fides, et Tuscis digna libellis, Quaeque coronata lustrari debeat agna:"

["Today, if a friend does not deny his trust, but returns the old purse with all its rust, it is a prodigious faith, worthy of being recorded in the Tuscan annals, and a garlanded lamb should be sacrificed to such exemplary integrity." — Juvenal, Sat., xiii. 60.]

There never was a time or place when princes could promise themselves more certain and greater rewards for virtue and justice. The first one who sets himself to win favour and esteem by these means, I am much deceived if he does not, by the best title, outstrip his competitors. Force and violence can do something, but not always everything. We see merchants, country justices, and craftsmen rivalling the best of the nobility in valour and military skill: they perform honourable actions in public engagements and in private quarrels; they fight duels; they defend towns in our present wars. A prince is smothered in this crowd of credit. Let him shine bright in humanity, truth, loyalty, temperance, and especially in justice — marks that are rare, unrecognised, exiled. It is by no other means than the simple goodwill of the people that he can do his business, and no other qualities can attract their goodwill like those, as being the most useful to them:
"Nil est tam populare, quam bonitas."
["Nothing is so popular as goodness." — Cicero, Pro Ligar., c. 12.]

By that standard I would have been great and rare, just as I find myself today small and common by the standard of certain past ages, when, if no other better qualities went along with them, it was ordinary and common to see a man moderate in his vengeance, gentle in resenting injuries, religious of his word, neither double nor pliant, not adjusting his faith to others' wishes or the turn of the times. I would rather see all affairs go to wreck and ruin than break my faith to save them. As for this new virtue of feigning and dissimulation, now in such credit, I mortally hate it; and of all vices I find none that shows so much baseness and meanness of spirit. It is a cowardly and servile humour to hide and disguise oneself under a mask, and not to dare to show oneself as one is. By this our servants are trained up in treachery: brought up to say what is not true, they make no conscience of a lie. A noble heart should not belie its own thoughts; it should let itself be seen within; all there is good, or at least human. Aristotle reckons it the office of magnanimity to love and hate openly, professedly; to judge and speak with all freedom; and not to value the approval or disapproval of others against the truth. Apollonius said that lying was for slaves, and truth-speaking for free men: it is the chief and fundamental part of virtue; we must love it for itself. The man who speaks truth because he is bound to, and because it serves him, and who is not afraid to lie when it matters to nobody, is not sufficiently true. My soul naturally abhors lying, and hates the very thought of it. I feel an inward shame and a sharp remorse if a lie ever escapes me — as it sometimes does, when I am surprised by occasions that give me no time to prepare. A man should not always tell everything, for that would be folly; but what a man says should be what he thinks, otherwise it is knavery. I do not understand what advantage men think they get from constant counterfeiting and dissimulating, if not never to be believed even when they speak the truth. It may pass with people once or twice; but to make a profession of concealing one's thought, and to brag, as some of our princes have done, that they would burn their shirts if they knew their true intentions (a saying of the old Metellus of Macedon), or that those who do not know how to dissemble do not know how to rule — that is to warn everyone who has dealings with them that everything they say is nothing but lying and deceit:
"Quo quis versutior et callidior est, hoc invisior et suspectior, detracto opinione probitatis:"
["The more cunning and crafty a man is, the more he is hated and suspected, once the reputation for integrity is gone." — Cicero, De Off., ii. 9.]

It would be very simple for anyone to put any stress on the countenance or word of a man who has made up his mind always to be outwardly other than he is within, as Tiberius did; and I cannot conceive what part such people can have in conversation with men, since nothing they produce is received as true: whoever is disloyal to truth is disloyal to falsehood too.

Those of our time who, in formulating the duty of a prince, have considered only the good of his affairs and have preferred that to the care of his faith and conscience, might have something to say to a prince whose affairs fortune had so placed that he could establish them forever by once breaking his word; but it does not work that way: they often buy in the same market; they make more than one peace and enter into more than one treaty in their lives. Gain tempts the first breach of faith, and almost always presents itself, as in all other bad acts — sacrileges, murders, rebellions, treasons — being undertaken for some kind of advantage. But this first gain has infinite ill consequences, throwing the prince out of all correspondence and negotiation by this example of infidelity. Soliman, of the Ottoman race — a race not very particular about keeping their words or compacts — when, in my infancy, he landed his army at Otranto, hearing that Mercurino de' Gattinara and the inhabitants of Castro were being held prisoner after having surrendered the place contrary to the articles of their capitulation, sent orders that they should be released, saying that, since he had other great enterprises in hand in those parts, the disloyalty, though it carried a show of present utility, would in future bring on him a disrepute and distrust of infinite prejudice.

For my part, I would rather be tiresome and indiscreet than a flatterer and a dissembler. I confess there may be some mixture of pride and obstinacy in keeping myself so upright and open, without any deference to others; I think I am perhaps a little too free where I should least be so, and that I grow hot in the face of respectful settings; and it may be that I follow the bent of my own nature for want of art, using the same liberty of speech and bearing towards great people that I bring with me from my own house. I am aware how much this verges on incivility and indiscretion; but besides being so bred, I do not have a wit nimble enough to evade a sudden question, or to escape by some dodge, nor to feign a truth, nor memory enough to retain such a feigning, nor truly the assurance to keep it up — so I play the brave out of weakness. And so I give myself up to candour, always speaking as I think, both by temperament and by design, leaving the outcome to fortune. Aristippus used to say that the chief benefit he had got out of philosophy was that he spoke freely and openly to everyone.

Memory is a wonderfully useful faculty, and without it judgment can hardly do its office. For my part I have none at all. Whatever anyone wishes to put to me must be done in pieces, for to answer a speech with several heads to it I am not able. I could not take a commission by word of mouth without a notebook. And when I have a speech of any importance to make, if it is long, I am reduced to the wretched necessity of learning it off by heart word for word; otherwise I would have neither method nor confidence, fearing that my memory would play me a slippery trick. But this method is no less difficult for me than the other: it takes me three hours to learn three lines. And besides, in a man's own work, the freedom and authority to change the order, alter a word, constantly vary the material, makes it stick less easily in the author's memory. The more I distrust it the worse it serves; it serves me best by accident, when I solicit it negligently. If I press it, it gets confused, and once it starts to falter, the more I sound it, the more it is perplexed. It serves me at its hour, not at mine.

The same defect I find in my memory I find in several other parts of me. I flee command, obligation, and constraint; what I can otherwise do naturally and easily, I cannot do once I have imposed it on myself by an express, strict injunction. Even the members of my body, which have a more particular jurisdiction of their own, sometimes refuse to obey me if I order them on duty at a fixed hour. This tyrannical, compulsory appointment baffles them; they shrink up, through fear or spite, and fall into a trance. Once, in a place where it is reckoned a barbarous discourtesy not to drink to those who drink to you, though I was given full liberty I tried to play the good fellow, out of respect to the ladies who were there, according to the custom of the country; but with all the pressure and preparation, forcing myself against my custom and inclination, my throat closed up so that I could not swallow a single drop, and I was deprived even of drinking with my meal. I found myself sated, my thirst quenched, by the imagined drink that my imagination had swallowed. This effect is most marked in those with the strongest and most powerful imagination, but it is natural to all, and there is no one who does not feel it in some measure. An excellent archer was offered his life, when condemned to die, if he would give some notable proof of his art; but he refused to try, fearing that the over-effort of his will might make him shoot wide, and that instead of saving his life he would also lose the reputation he had earned as a marksman. A man whose mind is on something else will not fail, in his walking, to take the same number and length of paces, down to an inch, in his usual place; but if he makes it his business to measure and count them, he will find that what he did by nature and by accident he cannot do so exactly by design.

My library, which is a fine one as village libraries go, is in a corner of my house. If anything comes into my head that I want to look up or write down, I am afraid I shall forget it just walking across the courtyard, and have to commit it to someone else's memory. If, in speaking, I venture the least bit from my subject, I am infallibly lost — which is why I keep myself strictly on the point in discourse. I am forced to call the men who serve me either by the names of their offices or their birthplace, for names are very hard for me to remember. I can tell, perhaps, that there are three syllables, that it has a harsh sound, that it begins or ends with a particular letter; but that is all. And if I lived long, I do not doubt I should forget my own name, as some others have done. Messala Corvinus was two years without any trace of memory, and the same is said of Georgius Trapezuntius. For my own interest, I often meditate on what kind of life theirs was, and whether, without this faculty, I should have enough left to support me with any tolerable ease; and looking narrowly into it, I fear this deprivation, if total, destroys all the other functions of the soul:
"Plenus rimarum sum, hac atque iliac perfluo."
["I am full of chinks, and leak out every way." — Terence, Eunuchus, ii. 2, 23.]

More than once I have forgotten the watchword I had been given or had given out three hours before, and forgotten where I had hidden my purse — whatever Cicero may say, I make a point of losing what I have taken particular care to lock up safely:
"Memoria certe non modo Philosophiam sed omnis vitae usum, omnesque artes, una maxime continet."
["It is certain that memory contains within itself not only philosophy, but all the uses of life and all the arts." — Cicero, Acad., ii. 7.]

Memory is the storehouse and case of science; mine being so treacherous, if I know little, I cannot complain much. I know, in general, the names of the arts and what they deal with, but no more. I turn over books; I do not study them. What I retain I no longer recognise as another's; it is only what my judgment has profited by, the discourses and ideas it has been instructed by — author, place, words, and other circumstances I forget immediately. I am so excellent at forgetting that I forget my own writings and compositions no less than the rest. I am very often quoted to myself and do not know it. Whoever should ask me where I got the verses and examples I have piled up here, would have me at a loss to tell him; and yet I have not borrowed them except from famous, known authors, not content that they should merely be rich, but wanting them rich and from honourable hands as well, where authority concurs with reason. It is no great wonder if my book runs the same fortune as other books, if my memory loses what I have written as well as what I have read, what I give as well as what I receive.

Besides the defect of memory, I have others that contribute much to my ignorance. I have a slow and heavy wit; the least cloud stops its progress, so that, for example, I never propose any easy riddle to it that it could solve; there is not the slightest piece of pointless subtlety that does not floor me; in games where wit is required, like chess, draughts, and the like, I understand no more than the basic moves. My apprehension is slow and tangled; but what it once does apprehend, it apprehends well, for as long as it retains it. My eyesight is sharp and clear, picking things out at a great distance, but soon grows tired and heavy at work, which is why I cannot read for long and have to have someone read to me. The younger Pliny can inform those who have not experienced it themselves how serious an impediment this is for people devoted to that kind of work.

There is no soul so wretched and coarse that some particular faculty does not show through; no soul so buried in sloth and ignorance that it will not sally out at one point or another. How it happens that a man blind and asleep to everything else turns out lively, clear, and excellent in some one particular effect, we may have to ask our masters. But the beautiful souls are those that are universal, open, ready for everything — if not yet instructed, at least capable of being so; which I say to accuse my own. For whether through infirmity or negligence (and to neglect what lies at our feet, what we have in our hands, what most closely concerns the use of life, is far from my doctrine), there is not a soul in the world so awkward as mine, and so ignorant of many common things — things that a man cannot, without shame, fail to know. I must give some examples.

I was born and raised in the country, among farmers; I have had business and husbandry in my own hands ever since my predecessors, who were lords of the estate I now hold, left me to succeed them; and yet I can neither cast accounts nor reckon my counters; I do not know most of our current money, nor the difference between one grain and another, either growing in the field or in the barn, if it is not too obvious. I can scarcely tell the cabbages from the lettuces in my garden. I do not even understand the names of the chief instruments of husbandry, nor the most ordinary basics of agriculture that children know; still less the mechanical arts, traffic, merchandise, the variety and nature of fruits, wines, and viands, nor how to make a hawk fly, nor to physic a horse or a dog. And, since I have to publish my whole shame, it is not above a month ago that I was caught out by my ignorance of the use of yeast in making bread, and of what end it serves to keep wine in the vat. In ancient Athens they guessed at an aptitude for mathematics in a man they saw skillfully tying up a bundle of brushwood. In earnest, they would draw a quite contrary conclusion from me, for give me all the provisions and equipment of a kitchen and I would starve. By these features of my confession, men may imagine others to my disadvantage; but whatever I make myself out to be, provided it is what I really am, I have my end. I will not make any excuse for committing such mean, frivolous things to paper: the meanness of the subject obliges me to it. They may, if they please, accuse my project, but not my carrying-out of it. So it is that, without anybody's needing to tell me, I see well enough how little weight and value all this has, and the folly of my design; it is enough that my judgment does not contradict itself — these are the essays of that.

"Nasutus sis usque licet, sis denique nasus, Quantum noluerit ferre rogatus Atlas; Et possis ipsum te deridere Latinum, Non potes in nugas dicere plura meas, Ipse ego quam dixi: quid dentem dente juvabit Rodere? carne opus est, si satur esse velis. Ne perdas operam; qui se mirantur, in illos Virus habe; nos haec novimus esse nihil."

["Let your nose be as keen as you will, be all nose, even a nose so great that Atlas would refuse to bear it; even if you could outdo Latinus himself in jeering, against my trifles you could say no more than I myself have said: then to what end tooth against tooth? You must have flesh, if you would be full; do not waste your labour; vent your venom on those who admire themselves; I know already that these things are worthless." — Martial, xiii. 2.]

I am under no obligation not to say absurdities, provided I am not deceived by them and know them for what they are. And to trip knowingly is so usual with me that I rarely do otherwise, and rarely trip by accident. It is no great matter to add ridiculous actions to the rashness of my humour, since I cannot usually help supplying it with vicious ones.

I was present one day at Bar-le-Duc when King Francis II was presented, as a memorial of René, king of Sicily, with a portrait the latter had drawn of himself. Why is it not equally lawful for anyone to portray himself with a pen, as he did with a crayon? I will not, then, leave out this blemish, very awkward as it is to publish: irresolution — a very great defect, and very inconvenient in the dealings of the world's affairs. In doubtful undertakings, I do not know which way to choose:
"Ne si, ne no, nel cor mi suona intero."
["Neither yes nor no rings whole in my heart." — Petrarch.]

I can maintain an opinion, but I cannot choose one. Since in human affairs, whatever side you incline to, many appearances offer themselves to confirm you in it, the philosopher Chrysippus said that he would learn from Zeno and Cleanthes, his masters, only their doctrines — he would find proofs and reasons of his own. Whichever way I turn, I never lack reasons and likelihoods to fix me there; so I keep doubt and the liberty of choice in suspense until the moment presses; and then, to tell the truth, for the most part I toss the feather into the wind, as the saying is, and commit myself to the mercy of fortune; a very slight inclination and circumstance carries me along with it.
"Dum in dubio est animus, paulo momento huc atque Illuc impellitur."
["While the mind is in doubt, the slightest impulse pushes it this way and that." — Terence, Andr., i. 6, 32.]

The uncertainty of my judgment is so evenly balanced in most occurrences that I could willingly leave it to be decided by the throw of a die; and I observe, with great pertinence to our human frailty, the examples left to us even by sacred history of this custom of referring to fortune and chance the decision of election in doubtful matters:
"Sors cecidit super Matthiam."
["The lot fell upon Matthias." — Acts i. 26.]

Human reason is a two-edged and dangerous sword: observe in the hands of Socrates, her most intimate and familiar friend, how many points it has. So I am good for nothing but to follow, and let myself be easily carried along with the crowd; I have not confidence enough in my own strength to take it upon myself to command and lead. I am very glad to find the way trodden by others before me. If I have to run the hazard of an uncertain choice, I would rather have it under someone more confident in his opinions than I am in mine, whose ground and foundation I find very slippery and unsure.
Yet I do not easily change, since I see the same weakness in the opposite opinions:
"Ipsa consuetudo assentiendi periculosa esse videtur, et lubrica;"
["The very habit of assenting seems dangerous and slippery." — Cicero, Acad., ii. 21.]
especially in political matters, there is a wide field open for shifts and disputes:
"Justa pari premitur veluti cum pondere libra, Prona, nec hac plus parte sedet, nec surgit ab illa."
["As a just balance, pressed with equal weight, neither dips nor rises on either side." — Tibullus, iv. 41.]

Machiavelli's writings, for example, were solid enough for their subject, but were easy enough to controvert; and those who did so left their own writings just as easy to controvert in turn. There has never been a lack of replies and replies upon replies in this kind of argument, and as endless a tangle of debates as our wrangling lawyers have spun out in long lawsuits:
"Caedimur et totidem plagis consumimus hostem;"
["We are cut down, and with as many blows we wear out the enemy" (or, "It is a fight in which we exhaust each other by mutual wounds"). — Horace, Epist., ii. 2, 97.]

the reasons have little other foundation than experience, and the variety of human events offers us infinite examples of every sort of form. A man of understanding in our day says: that whoever, contrary to our almanacs, would write "cold" where they say "hot," and "wet" where they say "dry," always putting the opposite of what they predict — if he had to lay a bet, he would not mind which side he took, except where no uncertainty was possible, as in promising extreme heat at Christmas or extreme cold at Midsummer. I think the same of these political controversies: whichever side you take, you have as fair a game to play as your opponent, provided you do not go so far as to clash with principles broad and manifest. And yet in my view, in public affairs, there is no government so bad that, provided it is ancient and has been steady, it is not better than change and alteration.

Our manners are infinitely corrupt, and tend wonderfully to get worse; of our laws and customs there are many that are barbarous and monstrous; nevertheless, because of the difficulty of reformation, and the danger of stirring things up, if I could put something under to stop the wheel and keep it where it is, I would do it with all my heart:
"Numquam adeo foedis, adeoque pudendis Utimur exemplis, ut non pejora supersint."
["The examples we use are never so shameful and foul but that worse remain behind." — Juvenal, viii. 183.]

The worst thing I find in our state is instability, and the fact that our laws, no more than our clothes, cannot settle into any fixed form. It is very easy to accuse a government of imperfection, for everything mortal is full of it; it is very easy to make a people contemptuous of ancient practices — no one ever undertook it without succeeding; but to establish a better order in place of the one a man has overthrown, many who have attempted it have come to grief. I consult my own prudence very little in my conduct; I am willing to let it be guided by the public rule. Happy the people who do what they are commanded better than those who command, without tormenting themselves about the causes, who let themselves be carried gently along on the celestial revolution! Obedience is never pure or calm in the man who reasons and disputes.

In short, to come back to myself: the only thing on which I somewhat esteem myself is what no man has ever thought himself defective in; my distinction is vulgar, common, and popular — for who ever thought he lacked sense? That would be a self-contradictory proposition; it is a disease that never exists where it is recognised; tenacious and strong it is, but the first ray of the patient's own eye nevertheless pierces and disperses it, as the sun's beams do thick, obscure mist. To accuse oneself in this matter would be to excuse oneself, and to condemn oneself would be to absolve. There never was a porter or the silliest girl who did not think they had sense enough to do their business. We readily enough concede in others an advantage in courage, strength, experience, dexterity, and beauty, but an advantage in judgment we yield to no one; and the reasonings that come purely from another's natural conclusions, we think, if we had only turned our thoughts that way, we should have found out as well as he. Knowledge, style, and such parts as we see in others' works, we are soon aware of, if they surpass our own; but for the simple products of the understanding, everyone thinks he could have found out the like in himself, and is hardly sensitive to the weight and difficulty involved, unless (and only with much ado) at an extreme and incomparable distance. So that anyone who could clearly discern the height of another's judgment would be able to raise his own to the same pitch. So this is a sort of exercise from which a man can expect very little praise; a kind of composition of small repute. And besides, whom do you write for? The learned, to whom the authority belongs of judging books, know no other value than that of learning, and allow no other proceeding of wit than that of erudition and art; if you have mistaken one of the Scipios for another, what is everything else you have to say worth? Whoever is ignorant of Aristotle is, by their rule, in some sort ignorant of himself; vulgar souls cannot discern the grace and force of a lofty and delicate style. Now these two sorts of people take up the world. The third sort, into whose hands you fall, of souls regular and strong of themselves, is so rare that it justly has neither name nor place among us; and it is so much time lost to aspire to it, or to try to please it.

It is commonly said that the justest portion Nature has given us of her gifts is that of sense, for there is no one who is not content with his share. Is that not reasonable? Anyone who could see beyond that would see beyond his sight. I think my opinions are good and sound, but who does not think the same of his own? One of the best proofs that mine are so is the slight esteem I have for myself; for had they not been very well assured, they would easily have let themselves be deceived by the peculiar affection I have for myself, since I place it almost entirely in myself and do not let much run out. All that others distribute among an infinite number of friends and acquaintances, to their glory and their grandeur, I dedicate to the repose of my own mind and to myself. What escapes from there is not properly by my direction:
"Mihi nempe valere et vivere doctus."
["Learned to do well for myself and live for myself." — Lucretius, v. 959.]

I find my opinions very bold and steady in condemning my own imperfection. To tell the truth, it is a subject on which I exercise my judgment as much as any other. The world always looks outward; I turn my sight inward, and there fix and employ it. I have no other business but myself. I am forever meditating on myself, considering and tasting myself. Other men's thoughts are always wandering abroad, if they will but see it; they are always going forwards:
"Nemo in sese tentat descendere;"
["No one tries to descend into himself." — Persius, iv. 23.]

For my part, I circulate within myself. This capacity for trying the truth, whatever it is, in myself, and this free humour of not subjecting my belief too easily, I owe principally to myself; for the strongest and most general ideas I have are those that, so to speak, were born with me — they are natural and entirely my own. I produced them crude and simple, with a strong and bold production, but a little muddled and imperfect; I have since established and fortified them with the authority of others and the sound examples of the ancients, in whom I have found judgment of the same stamp: these have given me a firmer hold, and a more evident enjoyment and possession of what I had already embraced. The reputation that everyone aims at, for vivacity and quickness of wit, I seek in regularity; the glory they aim at from a brilliant and signal action, or some particular excellence, I claim from order, correspondence, and tranquillity of opinions and manners:
"Omnino si quidquam est decorum, nihil est profecto magis, quam aequabilitas universae vitae, tum singularum actionum, quam conservare non possis, si, aliorum naturam imitans, omittas tuam."

["If anything is wholly seemly, nothing is more so than an evenness in the whole of life, and in each particular action, which you cannot keep up if, imitating others' natures, you abandon your own." — Cicero, De Off., i. 31.]

Here, then, you see in what degree I find myself guilty of this first part, which I said was the vice of presumption. As to the second, which consists in not having a sufficient esteem for others, I do not know whether I can excuse myself so well; but whatever comes of it, I am resolved to speak the truth. Whether, perhaps, it is that the continual time I have spent with the humours of the ancients, and the idea of those great souls of past ages, has put me out of taste both with others and with myself; or whether, in truth, the age we live in produces only very indifferent things, the fact is that I see nothing worthy of any great admiration. Indeed, I do not have so great a familiarity with many men as would be needed to make a right judgment of them, and those with whom my condition makes me most frequent are, for the most part, men who have little care for the culture of the soul, who look on honour as the sum of all blessings and valour as the height of all perfection.

What I see fine in others I very readily commend and esteem; indeed, I often say more in commendation of them than I think they really deserve, and let myself lie that far — for I cannot invent a false subject; my testimony is never wanting to my friends in what I think deserves praise, and where a foot is due, I am willing to give them a foot and a half; but to attribute to them qualities they do not have, I cannot do it, nor openly defend their imperfections. Indeed, I frankly give my very enemies their due testimony of honour: my affection changes, my judgment does not, and I never confuse my animosity with other circumstances foreign to it; I am so jealous of the liberty of my judgment that I can hardly part with it for any passion whatsoever. I do myself a greater injury in lying than I do him about whom I tell the lie. This commendable and generous custom is observed by the Persian nation, that they spoke of their mortal enemies, and those with whom they were at deadly war, as honourably and justly as their virtues deserved.

I have known plenty of men with several fine parts: one with wit, another with courage, another with address, another with conscience, another with eloquence; one with one science, another with another. But a generally great man, who has all these brave parts together, or any one of them to such a degree of excellence that we should admire him, or compare him with those we honour from times past — my fortune never brought me acquainted with. The greatest I have known, I mean for the natural parts of the soul, was Etienne de la Boétie; his was a full soul indeed, with a beautiful aspect on every side; a soul of the old stamp, that would have produced great effects if his fortune had so pleased — having added much to those great natural parts by learning and study.

But how it comes about I do not know, and yet it is certainly so: there is as much vanity and weakness of judgment in those who profess the greatest abilities, who take on learned callings and bookish employments, as in any other kind of men. Either because more is required and expected of them, and common defects are not excusable in them, or because the opinion they have of their own learning makes them bolder to expose and lay themselves too open, by which they lose and betray themselves. As a craftsman more clearly shows his lack of skill in a rich material he is working with, if he disgraces the work by bad handling and contrary to the rules required, than in some material of less value; and people are more displeased by a disproportion in a statue of gold than in one of plaster. So do these men when they advance things that in themselves and in their place would be good — but they use them without discrimination, honouring the memories at the expense of their understandings, and making themselves ridiculous by honouring Cicero, Galen, Ulpian, and St Jerome all in the same way.

I willingly fall again into the discourse of the vanity of our education, whose end is not to make us good and wise, but learned — and it has achieved that. It has not taught us to follow and embrace virtue and prudence, but it has impressed on us their derivation and etymology; we know how to decline Virtue, even if we do not know how to love her; if we do not know what prudence is really and in effect, by experience, we have it nevertheless by jargon and by heart. We are not content to know our neighbours' descent, kindred, and connections; we want to have them as our friends, too, and to establish a correspondence and an intelligence with them. But this education of ours has taught us definitions, divisions, and subdivisions of virtue, like so many surnames and branches of a genealogy, without any further care of setting up any familiarity or intimacy between her and us. For our initial instruction it has picked out, not the books that contain the soundest and truest opinions, but those that speak the best Greek and Latin, and by their fine words has instilled into our minds the vainest humours of antiquity.

A good education alters judgment and manners — as happened to Polemon, a lewd and debauched young Greek, who chanced to go and hear one of Xenocrates' lectures, and did not only note the reader's eloquence and learning, and bring away not just the knowledge of some fine matter, but a far more obvious and more solid profit: the sudden change and reformation of his former life. Whoever found such an effect of our schooling?
"Faciasne, quod olim Mutatus Polemon? ponas insignia morbi Fasciolas, cubital, focalia; potus ut ille Dicitur ex collo furtim carpsisse coronas, Postquam est impransi correptus voce magistri?"

["Will you do what reformed Polemon did of old? Lay aside the badges of your disease — garters, cushion, neckcloth — as he is said, in his cups, to have stealthily torn the garlands from his neck when he was struck by the words of that fasting teacher?" — Horace, Sat., ii. 3, 253.]

That seems to me the least contemptible condition of men which, by its plainness and simplicity, is set at the lowest level, and invites us to a more regular course. I find the rough manners and language of country people commonly better suited to the rule and prescription of true philosophy than those of our philosophers themselves:
"Plus sapit vulgus, quia tantum, quantum opus est, sapit."
["The common people are wiser, because they know only what they need to know." — Lactantius, Instit. Div., iii. 5.]

The most remarkable men, as I have judged from outward appearance (for to judge them according to my own method, I should have to penetrate a great deal deeper), for soldiers and military leadership, were the Duc de Guise, who died at Orléans, and the late Marshal Strozzi; and for men of great ability and uncommon virtue, Olivier and de l'Hospital, Chancellors of France. Poetry, in my opinion, has also flourished in this age of ours; we have plenty of very good craftsmen at the trade — D'Aurat, Beza, Buchanan, L'Hospital, Mondoré, Turnèbe. As to the French poets, I believe they have raised their art to the highest point it can ever reach; and in those parts of it where Ronsard and Du Bellay excel, I find them little inferior to ancient perfection. Adrien Turnèbe knew more, and knew what he did know better, than any man of his time, or long before him. The lives of the late Duke of Alva and of our Constable de Montmorency were both great and noble, and had many rare resemblances of fortune. But the beauty and glory of the death of the latter, in sight of Paris and of his king, in their service, against his nearest relations, at the head of an army victorious by his conduct, and by a sudden stroke, in such extreme old age — it deserves, I think, to be recorded among the most remarkable events of our time. As also the steady goodness, sweetness of manners, and conscientious ease of Monsieur de la Noue, in so great an injustice of armed parties (the true school of treason, inhumanity, and robbery) — where he always kept up the reputation of a great and experienced captain.
I have taken delight in publishing in several places the hopes I have of Marie de Gournay le Jars,
[She was adopted by him in 1588. See Léon Feugère's Mademoiselle de Gournay: 'Étude sur sa Vie et ses Ouvrages'.]

my adopted daughter, and certainly loved by me more than as a father; enveloped in my retreat and solitude as one of the best parts of my own being. I have no longer any regard to anything in this world but her. And if a man may presage from her youth, her soul will one day be capable of very great things, and among others of the perfection of that sacred friendship which we do not read that any of her sex has yet attained. The sincerity and solidity of her manners are already enough for it, and her affection toward me is more than superabundant — such that there is nothing more to be wished, except that the apprehension she has of my end, being now fifty-five years old, did not so much afflict her. The judgment she passed on my first Essays — being a woman, so young, alone in her country in this age, and the famous vehemence with which she loved me and longed for my acquaintance, solely from the esteem she had thence formed of me, before she had ever seen my face — is an incident very worthy of consideration.

Other virtues have had little or no credit in this age; but valour has become popular by our civil wars, and in this we have souls brave even to perfection, and in such great number that the choice is impossible to make.
This is all of extraordinary and uncommon grandeur that has so far come to my knowledge.
